# Compat ledger

> **The rule:** *Every upgrade must keep existing users' access intact — account/login, keys, and already-uploaded data. No change may force a re-enroll, re-key, re-upload, re-share, or reset.*

The **append-only** record of every intentional change to a frozen surface (see [`CHECKLIST.md`](CHECKLIST.md) for the twelve of them).

**Append only.** Do not edit or delete an existing entry — including the ones that record mistakes. An entry that says "we broke this" is the reason it does not happen twice.

When you change a format, you write an entry here *and* you keep the old fixture *and* you keep a read path that still opens it. The pre-push hook warns when a frozen surface moves without a ledger entry; the corpus lock and the golden tests are the hard gate.

## Entry template

Copy this block, fill it in, append it to the bottom.

```markdown
## YYYY-MM-DD — <surface> — <one-line summary>

| | |
|---|---|
| **Commit** | `<sha>` |
| **Surface** | <which of the twelve frozen surfaces> |
| **What changed** | <the format delta, in bytes/fields> |
| **Why it is backward compatible** | <the argument, not the assertion> |
| **How OLD data is still read** | <the concrete read path: file:function> |
| **Fixture that proves it** | `compat/fixtures/<area>/<name>` (old) + `<name>` (new) |
| **Automatic on upgrade?** | <yes + how; or the migration id> |
```

## 2026-07-14 — client on-disk state (#11) — KNOWN WEAK SPOT: `staging/<file_id>/record.json` is unversioned

| | |
|---|---|
| **Commit** | *(none — recorded, not fixed; frozen as-is by the compat gate)* |
| **Surface** | #11, client on-disk state — `client-app/upload_staging.rs` |
| **What changed** | Nothing. This entry records a **liability**, so that the next person to touch it cannot claim they did not know. |
| **The problem** | A resumable upload's `staging/<file_id>/record.json` is **plain, unversioned, unsealed JSON**. It carries no magic bytes and no version tag, so there is no way for a future reader to tell which shape it is looking at, and no way to reject an unknown one. Every other access-critical format in the system fails closed on an unknown version; this one cannot even ask the question. |
| **Blast radius** | An in-flight resumable upload of a large file. A user who is mid-upload across an upgrade loses that upload's staged state — they must re-upload. That is a "re-upload", which is exactly what the rule forbids. |
| **Why it is frozen as-is** | The gate pins the CURRENT shape with a golden fixture, so today's records keep opening. Retro-versioning it is a change to the format, which is the very thing that needs the version tag first. |
| **What the next change to it MUST do** | Add a version tag **before** changing anything else. Concretely: accept the current tag-less shape as v0 forever (a compat-read path), write the new shape with an explicit version, fail closed on unknown versions, add a fixture for the new shape, and append an entry here. Do not "just add a field" — a tag-less format cannot safely gain a required one. |
| **Fixture** | `compat/fixtures/client-state/` (staging record — frozen at its current, unversioned shape) |

## 2026-07-11 — directory binding (#5/#10) — HISTORICAL BREAK (pre-gate): `2a626d6` forced a re-enroll

**This entry records a rule violation that already shipped.** It predates the gate. It is here so it is never repeated, and it is the reason the gate exists.

| | |
|---|---|
| **Commit** | `2a626d6` — "PQ-enrollment publish fix" |
| **Surface** | Directory binding / enrollment (`server/http.rs` `RegisterReq`, client `register.rs`) |
| **What changed** | User enrollment (`POST /v1/users`) never published the client's ML-KEM key into the signed directory binding: the client omitted `mlkem_pub_b64` and the server's `RegisterReq` had no such field, hard-coding `mlkem_pub: None`. Every binding was therefore classical while uploads had already moved to V2 hybrid wraps. The fix added the field on both sides. |
| **Why it was NOT backward compatible** | **It was not retroactive.** New enrollments got a hybrid binding; the bindings of everyone who had *already* enrolled were never republished and stayed classical. Every V2 reshare to them failed with `pq_key_missing`. |
| **Cost to users** | **Every already-enrolled recipient had to RE-ENROLL.** A forced re-enroll is a forbidden outcome under the rule. |
| **What should have happened** | Either (a) republish existing bindings automatically as part of the upgrade — a migration, not a manual step — or (b) keep a working reshare path to a classical binding so that old recipients kept receiving shares while their bindings caught up. Either would have satisfied the rule. Both were skipped because nothing was watching. |
| **Why nothing caught it** | Every test round-tripped: it sealed and opened with the same code, so both sides drifted together and the suite stayed green. There was no test that took an OLD binding and asked whether TODAY's code could still reshare to it. |
| **What now catches it** | The interop matrix (`crates/compat/tests/interop_matrix.rs`): every frozen `Suite` (V1 classical, V2 hybrid) × every frozen keyblob version (v1 classical, v2 PQ) must still unwrap, verify and **reshare**. It reproduces the break as its real symptom — *an old classical binding can no longer participate in a reshare* — not as a missing JSON field. |
| **Status** | Not retro-fixed; the affected recipients have already re-enrolled. Out of scope by decision (design spec §8). Recorded permanently. |

## 2026-07-14 — deployment env (systemd unit) — the SECOND fresh-install-only hole, closed

| | |
|---|---|
| **Commit** | `feat/compat-gate` |
| **Surface** | Deployment environment — `scripts/install-server.sh`, `scripts/upgrade-server.sh`, `crates/portable-server/src/config.rs` |
| **The hole** | `install-server.sh` writes the unit's `Environment=` lines; `upgrade-server.sh` never rewrote that unit (it only appended a `capacity.conf` drop-in). So **a new `MAXSECU_*` var reached fresh installs only — every already-deployed server kept its original unit forever.** Identical shape to the `docs/schema.sql`-on-fresh-install-only hole. Latent, not yet a live break: every var happened to have a safe default in `LauncherConfig::from_env`. |
| **What changed** | `MAXSECU_ENV_VARS` in `config.rs` is now the single source of truth (15 vars incl. `DATABASE_URL`). Both scripts carry matching tables (`SERVER_ENV_SURFACE` / `SERVER_ENV_RECONCILE`). `upgrade-server.sh` reconciles an existing unit with a `10-maxsecu-env.conf` drop-in containing **only vars missing everywhere**. |
| **Why it is backward compatible** | **Nothing an operator set is ever overwritten.** Drop-ins are applied *after* the base unit, so re-emitting an already-set name would override the operator — the opposite of the goal. We therefore write only names absent from the base unit, every other drop-in, and every `EnvironmentFile`. Every value written equals the compiled-in default, i.e. exactly what that server was already running with. `DATABASE_URL` (per-install random password), `MAXSECU_DATA_DIR` (synthesizing a path would MOVE the data dir → new cert, every pinned client locked out, empty blob store), `MAXSECU_PUBLIC_ADDR` (absence is meaningful) and the Dropbox secrets are **never synthesized** — each `-` in the table carries a written reason. |
| **Automatic on upgrade?** | Yes — step 7b of `upgrade-server.sh`. Idempotent (a second run is byte-identical, "already reconciled — no change"). |
| **Proven by** | `crates/compat/tests/env_surface.rs` (7 `compat_*` tests): a var the server reads that is not declared, or is declared but wired into only one of the two deployment paths, fails the gate. Plus a harness that runs the reconcile block **verbatim** from the shipped script against mock units: operator values survive untouched, a second run is a no-op, secrets never leave the 0600 `EnvironmentFile`. |
| **Also fixed** | `--reset` never removed the drop-in dir (a stale `capacity.conf` survived a "back to zero" reset and silently overrode the reinstall); a re-run of `install-server.sh` now clears the reconcile drop-in (else it would silently override a new `--port`). |

## 2026-07-14 — server `file_versions.alg` — records the manifest's real suite (was hardcoded `1`)

| | |
|---|---|
| **Commit** | `feat/compat-gate` |
| **Surface** | Server DB row (not a signed format) — `crates/server/src/files.rs` `parse_stage` |
| **What changed** | `alg: 1` was written unconditionally, so every `Suite::V2` (PQ-hybrid) file was recorded in the server's row as V1/classical — a lie in the database. Now it records the decoded manifest's actual suite, via an exhaustive match (a future `Suite::V3` fails to compile here rather than silently mis-recording). |
| **Why it is backward compatible** | **The column has no authoritative reader.** Traced end to end: it is never `SELECT`ed (every `FROM file_versions` reads `finalized` / `manifest_bytes` / `manifest_sig` / `owner_id`), `MemoryStore` does not even store it, `FileView`/`FileRes` have no `alg` field, no HTTP response body carries it, and the client takes the suite from the **signed manifest** it re-decodes. Old rows stay wrong and new rows are right, but both are inert — so fixing the writer creates no old/new divergence. **Had a reader existed, fixing the writer alone would have created a NEW divergence, and that would have been worse than the bug.** |
| **How OLD data is still read** | Unchanged: `client-core/download.rs:309`, `reshare.rs:139` read `manifest.alg` from the signed bytes. |
| **Not retro-fixed** | Existing rows keep `alg = 1`. Safe per the above; no re-upload, no re-key, no re-share. |
| **Next one of these** | `pg.rs:902` and `pg.rs:1258` hardcode `wrap_alg: 1` on the **read** side — the mirror-image bug. Harmless today for the same reason. Not fixed. |

## 2026-07-14 — `POST /v1/session/proof` — reports the configured session TTL (was hardcoded `3600`)

| | |
|---|---|
| **Commit** | `feat/compat-gate` |
| **Surface** | #10, `/v1` HTTP JSON — `crates/server/src/http.rs` |
| **What changed** | Login returned a hardcoded `expires_in_s: 3600` while the recovery path reported the real `session_ttl_ms / 1000`. The two disagreed. Both now share one `session_expires_in_s(ttl_ms)`, so they cannot drift apart again. |
| **Why it is backward compatible** | **Value-only change; the wire shape is identical** — `expires_in_s` is still present and still a JSON number, so every frozen HTTP golden still passes (they pin the key and type). At the default TTL the value is still literally `3600`. The client parses it as `u64` and hard-fails login if it is missing or non-numeric; both still hold. |
| **Rounding** | Floor, clamped to ≥1s for a non-zero TTL. Rounding *up* would re-introduce the very lie being fixed (a client trusting a token the server already killed); a sub-second TTL flooring to `0` reads as "already expired" and could drive a re-auth hot loop. |

## 2026-07-14 — GATE HARDENING — the schema-equivalence test could pass VACUOUSLY

**This entry records a bug found *in the gate itself*, on its first run against a live Postgres.**

| | |
|---|---|
| **Commit** | `feat/compat-gate` |
| **Surface** | The gate — `crates/compat/tests/schema_equivalence.rs` |
| **The bug** | Nothing asserted the introspection queries returned any rows. `fresh == upgraded` is **trivially true when both are empty**, so a probe that silently matched nothing — a typo'd predicate, a `search_path` regression, a future PG catalog change — would have produced a green gate that compared *nothing at all*. Worse: `A == B` is also satisfied when **both** paths have LOST the append-only triggers, so equality alone never proved append-only still exists. |
| **Fix** | A per-aspect non-empty guard, plus an explicit presence check for `maxsecu_forbid_update_delete` / `maxsecu_forbid_delete`. Proven by sabotaging a query to match zero rows: it now fails loudly, and **without the guard that sabotage passed silently.** |
| **Why this matters beyond the DB** | It is the same failure the whole gate exists to prevent — a test that is green because it is not looking. Any future compat probe must assert it found something. |
| **Also proven on live PG** | Gutting a trigger's plpgsql body (`RAISE EXCEPTION` → `RETURN NEW`) leaves `pg_get_triggerdef` **byte-identical** — the `TRIGGERS` comparison does not diverge, and only the trigger-function-body comparison catches it. Without that aspect, append-only would silently disappear from upgraded servers while the gate stayed green. |

## 2026-07-16 — server backup & rollback — NEW frozen surface #12 (`MXBU`), + additive `type_id 0x000F` (#5) and migration `0002` (#9)

The server-backup / rollback feature (design: `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-07-16-server-backup-rollback-design.md`) introduces one **new** frozen surface and makes two **additive** extensions to existing ones. Every part is additive — a new reader for new bytes; no old data is touched, re-shaped, re-required, or made unreadable — so nothing here can strand an existing user.

| | |
|---|---|
| **Commit** | *(server backup & rollback; design `37283fd`)* |
| **Surface** | **#12 (new)** `MXBU` sealed server-backup bundle; **#5 (additive)** canonical `type_id`; **#9 (additive)** DB schema |
| **What changed** | **(a) New surface #12 — `MXBU` v1** (`crates/server/src/backup/format.rs`): a passphrase-sealed (Argon2id + AES-256-GCM) bundle that carries the run-state an operator needs to roll back / rebuild — TLS key, operational signing seed, Dropbox token, and a `pg_dump`. It rides the cold tier next to blobs, so it must arrive already sealed. Layout: a 45-byte header (`magic "MXBU" ‖ version=1 ‖ m_kib ‖ t ‖ p ‖ salt[16] ‖ nonce_base[12]`), one header per **component** (a fresh salt + `nonce_base` per component — never one per backup, which would be a two-time pad), part AAD = `header ‖ part_index u32 BE ‖ is_last u8`, and nonce = `nonce_base` with `part_index.to_be_bytes()` XORed into bytes `8..12` (the TLS 1.3 record-nonce construction). A stored part blob is `header ‖ part_ct` — that same header is **repeated on every part**, so a part fetched off an untrusted tier is self-describing; the key is derived once from part 0's header and `MxbuOpener::open_part` refuses any part whose 45-byte prefix is not byte-identical to it, which is what stops a part of one bundle being spliced into another. **(b) Additive to #5** — one new `encoding` `type_id`, **`0x000F` = `BackupIndex`** (the bundle's authenticated table of contents), taking the registry 13 → **14** `type_id`s. **No new `labels::*`** — the container is never signed, so it needs no domain-separation label (labels stay 13). `0x000E` was already taken by `BundleBody`, so the next free id is `0x000F`. **(c) Additive to #9** — `migrations/0002_delete_tombstones.sql` adds two append-only tables, `file_tombstones` and `wrap_revocations`, so a DB **merge** can tell "missing because a user deleted / revoked it on purpose" from "missing because it was lost" (16 tables / 8 triggers total; both reuse the shared `maxsecu_forbid_update_delete` guard, so no new trigger function). |
| **Why it is backward compatible** | **All additive, in spirit and in bytes.** (a) `MXBU` is a brand-new format written to a brand-new cold-tier prefix (`_backup/<stamp>/…`); no pre-existing bytes are `MXBU`, and a real `blob_ref` always begins with 32 hex chars (`files.rs:414`), so `_backup` can never collide with — or shadow — a user's chunk. `unseal` reads `(m,t,p)` from the header and passes them through (it does **not** pin `ARGON2_DESKTOP_TARGET`), and the 12-char passphrase minimum gates **seal only** — both are deliberate widenings so a future Argon retune or a raised minimum never bricks a bundle already sitting in Dropbox. (b) A new `type_id` is purely additive: every existing struct keeps its id and its bytes; `0x000F` is a name that was never used before, and `is_registered()` already accepts it. (c) `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS` migrations that add tables no old row references — no column added to an existing table, nothing made `NOT NULL`, no existing row read or rewritten. The merge that consumes the tombstones is a **restore-time** reader; forward-only operation is untouched. |
| **How OLD data is still read** | Unchanged. `MXBU` is new, so there is no "old `MXBU`" to read; the frozen fixture proves today's reader opens an independently-written bundle forever. Every pre-`0x000F` `type_id` still decodes (the `canonical_vectors.tsv` + per-struct locks), and a fresh install still equals baseline + `0001` + `0002` (`compat_fresh_install_equals_upgraded_install`, live PG). |
| **Fixtures that prove it** | `compat/fixtures/backup/backup_v1.bin` (+ `.passphrase.txt` + `.expect.json`) — a 2-part `MXBU` bundle minted from the documented layout by `compat_emit_backup_fixtures`, opened forever by `golden_open::compat_frozen_backup_still_unseals`. `compat/fixtures/backup/backup_index_v1.bin` (+ `.expect.json`) — the `0x000F` container's **wire framing**, minted by the same emitter from `encoding-spec.md` §4 rather than by `encode()`, and decoded forever by `golden_open::compat_frozen_backup_index_still_decodes`. The two are separate on purpose: the seal fixture's part plaintexts are prose, so no byte of it constrains how a `BackupIndex` is framed, and a reordering of `entries` against `parts` would round-trip cleanly through `encode`/`decode` while leaving every bundle already on a cold tier with an undecodable part 0. Value locks: `value_locks::compat_type_ids_are_frozen` pins `BackupIndex = 0x000F`; `compat_mxbu_mxd5_mxkb_are_mutually_unopenable` (a differential magic probe) pins that `MXBU` never opens as `MXD5`/`MXKB` and vice-versa; `compat_backup_prefix_cannot_collide_with_a_blob_ref` pins the 32-hex `blob_ref` shape. Schema: `schema_equivalence::compat_fresh_install_equals_upgraded_install` (generic over `migrations()` — picked `0002` up with no code change). |
| **Automatic on upgrade?** | Yes — `0002` is applied by `scripts/upgrade-server.sh` (the standard `migrations/apply.sh` path, one transaction with its `schema_migrations` row, crash-safe and idempotent). The `MXBU` format and `0x000F` are code, live from the upgraded binary; no data migration is needed because nothing pre-existing is in either format. |

## 2026-08-01 — `/v1` HTTP JSON (#10) — the recovery principal is admitted on five existing routes (`403` → `200`)

**No bytes moved.** No route was added or removed, no request or response key changed, no status code changed for any *existing* caller. What changed is the **authorization semantics** of five already-frozen routes for **one** principal — the reserved `RECOVERY_ID`. It is logged here because the checklist previously said nothing about authorization at all, and that silence is exactly how a change like this slips past a byte-oriented gate.

**Sharing (`add_wrap`) is NOT part of this entry.** A draft of it said six routes and counted `add_wrap` among them; that was written against a design that was then **reverted before anything landed**. The route stays on `AuthedSession` and still `403`s recovery. The reason is this ledger's own rule — admitting it *destroys an existing user's access* — and it is written out in the **"What was deliberately NOT admitted"** row below rather than left as an omission, because an unexplained gap is how it gets "fixed" by someone next month.

| | |
|---|---|
| **Commit** | *(recovery browse/read session; working tree — operator decision recorded in `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-07-03-trusted-server-recovery-registration-design.md` §0 D6, AMENDED 2026-08-01)* |
| **Surface** | #10, `/v1` HTTP JSON — `crates/server/src/http.rs` |
| **What changed** | A second session extractor, `RecoveryOkSession`, admits every authenticated principal **including `RECOVERY_ID`**, and is applied to an explicit **five**-handler allowlist: `list_files` (`GET /v1/files`), `get_file` (`GET /v1/files/{id}`), `get_chunk` (`GET …/chunks/{i}`), `chunk_status` (`GET …/chunks/{i}/status`) and `logout` (`POST /v1/session/logout`). A recovery session previously got `403` from all five; it now gets the ordinary answer. So the shipped capability is: **browse every file, open/stream/download every file, end the session** — on top of the admin server actions it already had (minting user-role registration keys, unchanged since T5). `AuthedSession` is **unchanged** and still hard-`403`s `RECOVERY_ID`, so `create_file`, `stage_version`, `put_chunk`, `finalize_version`, **`add_wrap`**, `delete_wrap`, `discard_file`, `direct_link` and `list_recipients` — and every file endpoint added in future — stay barred. Always on; no config flag. |
| **What was deliberately NOT admitted (`add_wrap` — sharing)** | **Sharing does not ship, and the reason is this document's own rule.** `add_wrap` (`POST /v1/files/{id}/wraps`) was admitted in a draft and **reverted** to `AuthedSession` before anything landed, because admitting it *strands an existing user*: (a) the store's `add_wrap` is idempotent **by REPLACE** — it drops any existing row for that `recipient_id` before inserting — so a recovery re-share to somebody who **already had working access** swaps their good grant for a new one; and (b) that new grant is **unopenable**: `client-core`'s download path field-binds the ancestor before the chain walk and rejects any ancestor whose `recipient_type` is not `User`, and `granted_by = RECOVERY_ID` resolves to **no trusted signing key anywhere** (the embedded recovery pin carries `enc_pub` + optional `mlkem_pub` and **no `sig_pub`**), so the walk ends in `GrantChainBroken`. Net effect of the reverted design: **a recovery "share" silently and irreversibly destroys a recipient's access to data they already uploaded** — the exact failure this ledger exists to prevent, and a *worse* one than `2a626d6` because there is no re-enroll that repairs it. Note the direction: because nothing was ever shipped admitting `add_wrap`, holding it back is **not** a tightening and needs no add-only treatment. Actually shipping it later **is** the widening, and it may not ship until *both* of these exist: **(1) a trust anchor for a recovery-issued grant** — either publish a directory binding for `RECOVERY_ID` carrying a real Ed25519 signing key, or add `sig_pub` to the recovery pin and terminate the chain at the `DESIGN.md` §12.7 admin key (the pin is frozen surface #7, so option 2 is itself a format change and needs its own entry here); **and (2) a server-side refusal of a REPLACE when `granted_by == RECOVERY_ID`**, so that even a correct grant can only ADD access, never overwrite it. The client also refuses (`recovery_share_unsupported`, `client-app/commands/share.rs`), but a client-side refusal is not a security boundary — the bar is the extractor. |
| **Why it is backward compatible** | **This is a widening, and the checklist's rule is prefer widening over tightening.** Concretely: (a) **no existing caller's outcome changes.** The only principal whose result moves is `RECOVERY_ID`, which is the reserved all-zero `Id` — server-assigned user ids are `random_array::<16>()`, so no real user can ever hold it (residual R1 in `docs/security-review-trusted-server-recovery.md`, 2⁻¹²⁸). Every ordinary user's request takes byte-identical code and returns a byte-identical response. (b) **The direction is `403` → `200`/`404`.** Loosening a caller check can only make previously-refused calls succeed; it cannot strand anyone, because nothing that worked stops working. The break-shaped version of this change would be the mirror image — moving a handler *from* `RecoveryOkSession` *to* `AuthedSession` **after it had shipped that way** — which is a tightening and would need the full add-only treatment. (The `add_wrap` revert described below is *not* that case: it never shipped admitted, so no deployed caller ever saw it succeed.) (c) **No wire shape moved.** `my_wrap.wrapped_dek_b64` and the rest of the §8.5 body already exist in the frozen fixture (`compat/fixtures/http/files_get.res.json` — `my_wrap.{wrapped_dek_b64,grant_b64,grant_sig_b64,ancestor_grants}`), and a recovery caller is served through **the same** `Store::get_file(file_id, selector, caller_id)` path as anyone else: the store selects the wrap whose `recipient_id == caller_id`, so recovery receives the recovery wrap **in the existing `my_wrap` field**. No new key, no changed type, no new required request field. (d) **No fixture pinned the old `403`.** `crates/compat/tests/http_wire.rs` dispatches the frozen route surface **with no session token** and asserts only `!= 404 && != 405` (`compat_route_surface_is_a_superset`), and no test in the compat crate mints a `RECOVERY_ID` session at all — so the corpus never recorded the refusal that changed. |
| **How OLD data is still read** | Unchanged. This touches no stored format. Old clients call the same routes with the same bodies and receive the same responses; a shipped client that never logs in as recovery cannot observe the change. |
| **Fixture that proves it** | No new fixture — nothing in the corpus constrains authorization, which is the point of the CHECKLIST sentence added alongside this entry. The behaviour is pinned instead by `crates/server/tests/recovery_login_e2e.rs`, which asserts **both halves**: the admitted routes answer `200`/`404` rather than `403`, and `create_file` / `stage_version` / `finalize_version` / `add_wrap` / `delete_wrap` / `discard_file` / `list_recipients` / `direct_link` still answer `403`. The `add_wrap` assertion is the load-bearing one — it posts a **well-formed** wrap body (so a `403` cannot be mistaken for a parse failure) and will fail the moment somebody admits the route, which is the intended trip-wire. Route existence and JSON shape stay pinned by `compat/fixtures/http/{routes.json,files_get.res.json,files_list.res.json,files_add_wrap.req.json}`. |
| **Automatic on upgrade?** | Yes — code only, live from the upgraded binary. No migration, no operator step, no client change. |
| **The security cost (recorded here on purpose)** | Compat-safe is not the same as risk-free, and holding `add_wrap` back does **not** make this cheap. **Recovery key + network reach now yields complete, remote plaintext of every file, with no operator involvement and no ceremony** — previously that same key-holder had to convene the air-gapped `DESIGN.md` §12.7 ceremony to read a *single* file. The delta is **reach, not identity** (a session is TLS-exporter-bound and can only be minted by a holder of the recovery *private* keys), but reach is the whole of it: **reads are neither audited nor rate-limited** — no read path in this server is, for any principal — so a bulk escrow browse of the entire corpus leaves **no trace at all**. And `get_chunk` is not side-effect-free when a cold tier is configured: it rehydrates and may offload capacity victims, exactly as for an ordinary caller. What this entry does **not** buy is grant power: recovery cannot make another account a reader of anything (`add_wrap` → `403`, see the row above). Deliberate, operator-approved; see spec §0 D6 and the 2026-08-01 addendum in `docs/security-review-trusted-server-recovery.md`. |

## 2026-08-02 — `/v1` HTTP JSON (#10) — TIGHTENING: `DELETE …/wraps/{recovery_id}` is refused for every caller (`204` → `403 recovery_protected`)

**This is a tightening, and it is logged as one.** [`CHECKLIST.md`](CHECKLIST.md)'s surface-#10 row says it in as many words: *a caller that used to succeed now getting a `403` is a **break**, and no golden fixture will catch it for you.* This one is judged safe on evidence, not on intent — the evidence is below.

| | |
|---|---|
| **Commit** | *(working tree — uncommitted; F2 of the prod-upgrade loop)* |
| **Surface** | #10, `/v1` HTTP JSON — `DELETE /v1/files/{file_id}/wraps/{recipient_id}` |
| **What changed** | Targeting the **recovery recipient** is now refused for **every** caller, the file owner included: `403` with a body `{"code":"recovery_protected"}`. "The recovery recipient" means either the path id `00000000000000000000000000000000` (`RECOVERY_ID`) **or** a stored wrap whose `recipient_type = 2`. Three layers: the HTTP handler *before* the audit edge (`crates/server/src/http.rs:1890`, helper at `:1927`), `MemoryStore` before the lock and again on the stored type (`crates/server/src/store.rs:1244`, `:1266`), and `PgStore` **before `pool.begin()`** plus a stored-type check ahead of every write inside the txn (`crates/server/src/pg.rs:1232`, `:1286`). New error variant `DeleteWrapError::RecoveryProtected` (`crates/server/src/files.rs:249`). Ordinary `403`s on this route stay **bodiless** — only this refusal carries a code. |
| **Why the refusal exists** | Stripping the recovery wrap is a **one-way blinding of the escrow**. `add_wrap` hard-rejects `recipient_id == RECOVERY_ID` in both stores (`crates/server/src/store.rs:1205`, `crates/server/src/pg.rs:1150-1151`), so nothing can put the wrap back at that version — not the owner, not the operator. On Postgres the same request additionally writes an **append-only `wrap_revocations` tombstone** (`crates/server/src/pg.rs:1307-1310`; table + immutability trigger at `migrations/0002_delete_tombstones.sql:74,82-84`) that can never be removed, so even a backup restore honours the blinding. `DESIGN.md` §1.2/§6.3 claim the escrow "can decrypt 100% of all files, past and present"; while this call succeeded that claim was **false**, and the failure was silent and permanent. |
| **Why the tightening is safe** | **No shipped client has ever issued this call.** Verified by grep, not by assertion: `delete_req` has exactly two call sites in the client — `crates/client-app/src/commands/delete_cmd.rs:54-59` and `crates/client-app/src/commands/upload.rs:1782-1783` — and **both** build the URI `"/v1/files/{file_id_hex}"`, the §8.7 file-delete route, never `…/wraps/…`. `tools/live-smoke` has none. So no deployed caller's outcome changes. Second: this rejects one **future request**; it makes **no stored byte unreadable** and costs nobody a re-enroll, re-key, re-upload or re-share. Third, the direction is the protective one — the refusal *preserves* access (to the escrow) rather than removing it. |
| **Why `403` and not `400`** | Deliberately asymmetric with `add_wrap`, which answers `400` for the same recipient. There the **body** is invalid (a re-share may never target recovery, §12.9). Here the request is well-formed and the caller **is** authorized for the route — just not for this target, which is what `403` means. `403` is already in this route's frozen response set, so the status code itself is not new to any caller. Reasoned out at `crates/server/src/files.rs:243-249`. |
| **How OLD data is still read** | Unchanged — this touches no stored format. A wrap row already deleted by the old behaviour stays deleted; nothing retro-scans. |
| **Fixture that proves it** | No new fixture: no bytes moved, and the corpus does not constrain authorization (the same gap the 2026-08-01 entry records). The frozen route fixture `compat/fixtures/http/routes.json:108-111` still dispatches this route and still passes, because `compat_route_surface_is_a_superset` sends **no session token** — it `401`s before the handler and never reaches the guard. Behaviour is pinned instead by `crates/server/tests/sharing.rs:230` (owner refused, wrap survives), `:263` (an ordinary recipient is still revocable — no over-blocking), `crates/server/tests/pg_store.rs:1919` (the load-bearing one: over a **fresh pool**, the wrap row survives **and** `SELECT count(*) FROM wrap_revocations == 0`, so no tombstone was left behind by a rolled-back txn) and `crates/server/tests/recovery_login_e2e.rs:657` (real TLS: `403` + `recovery_protected` on the recovery id, while the SAME caller on the SAME nonexistent file with an ordinary recipient gets `404` — proving the `403` is about the target, not the caller). |
| **Automatic on upgrade?** | Yes — code only, live from the upgraded binary. No migration, no operator step, no client change. |

## 2026-08-02 — `/v1` HTTP JSON (#10) — TIGHTENING: a stage's recovery wrap must set BOTH halves or NEITHER (`201`/`500` → `400`)

| | |
|---|---|
| **Commit** | *(working tree — uncommitted; F5.3 of the prod-upgrade loop)* |
| **Surface** | #10, `/v1` HTTP JSON — `POST /v1/files` and `POST /v1/files/{id}/versions` (`parse_stage`) |
| **What changed** | The "is this the recovery wrap?" test changed from an **OR** to the **biconditional** `recipient_type == 2 ⇔ recipient_id == RECOVERY_ID`, applied to **every** wrap in the body (`crates/server/src/files.rs:411-431`), mirrored in `MemoryStore::stage_version` before any row lands (`crates/server/src/store.rs:922-932`). A **half-shape** — a wrap claiming `recipient_type = 2` addressed to a real user id, or one claiming the all-zero sentinel id under `recipient_type = 1` — is now `400`, via the new `StageError::MismatchedRecoveryWrap` (`crates/server/src/files.rs:157`, mapped at `crates/server/src/http.rs:1255`). |
| **Status-code delta, stated exactly** | On **Postgres**: `500` → `400`. The row was **already refused** — it violates the `file_key_wraps` CHECK — but it surfaced as an opaque backend fault. On **MemoryStore**: `201` → `400`. That is the real tightening, and it only ever affected a MemoryStore-backed server (`--ephemeral` dev / tests), never a deployed one. |
| **Why the tightening is safe** | Four independent pieces of evidence that **no real client has ever written this shape, and no deployment ever accepted it**: (1) **Postgres has rejected it since the baseline** — `CHECK ( (recipient_type = 2) = (recipient_id = decode('00000000000000000000000000000000','hex')) )` at `migrations/0001_baseline.sql:253` (mirrored `docs/schema.sql:238`). Every production server is `PgStore`, so no half-shape wrap exists in any real database and none can be created. (2) **`maxsecu_encoding` refuses to DECODE the matching `Grant`** — `DecodeError::RecoveryIdMismatch` at `crates/encoding/src/structs.rs:202-205` — so the signed grant riding alongside such a wrap is unparseable and the wrap is inert wherever it lands. (3) **The shipped client hardcodes the correct pairing**: `crates/client-app/src/commands/upload.rs:138-143` — `let rid = if w.recipient_type == "recovery" { "recovery" } else { hex16(...) }` — and the server maps the literal `"recovery"` to `RECOVERY_ID` at `crates/server/src/http.rs:1147-1153`. The two halves cannot come apart on the shipped path. (4) The frozen request fixture `compat/fixtures/http/files_add_wrap.req.json` and the rest of the HTTP corpus still pass (`cargo test -p maxsecu-compat --locked` green, no fixture edited). |
| **What the OR let through, and why it mattered** | The old test accepted a "recovery wrap" addressed to a **real user id**. On a MemoryStore-backed server that file was accepted (`201`) with **nothing the escrow key can open** — silently and permanently unrecoverable, the mirror image of the F2 entry above. Widening was not an option here: the safe shape is the one Postgres has enforced all along, so this is the server catching up to its own schema, not a new rule. |
| **How OLD data is still read** | Unchanged. No stored wrap is re-validated; the check runs only on a **new** stage. Every wrap already in a real database satisfies the biconditional by construction (the CHECK). |
| **Fixture that proves it** | No new fixture — no bytes format changed, only which request bodies are refused. Pinned by three unit tests at `crates/server/src/files.rs:761-813` (both half-shapes → `MismatchedRecoveryWrap`; the correct pair still accepted). |
| **Automatic on upgrade?** | Yes — code only. No migration, no operator step, no client change. |

## 2026-08-02 — `/v1` HTTP JSON (#10) — WIDENING: `GET /v1/files` gains `offset`/`cursor`/`sort`/`owner`, a populated `next_cursor` and a new `total`

| | |
|---|---|
| **Commit** | *(working tree — uncommitted; F3/F3a of the prod-upgrade loop)* |
| **Surface** | #10, `/v1` HTTP JSON — `GET /v1/files`; plus the Tauri-internal `list_feed` seam, which is **not** a frozen surface (see below) |
| **What changed (server)** | Four **new, all-optional** query parameters on `ListQuery` (`crates/server/src/http.rs:2045-2066`): `offset` (u32, default 0), `cursor` (opaque; supersedes `offset` when present and valid), `sort` (`newest` default \| `oldest`), `owner` (`me` only). The response gains a new integer `total` (`crates/server/src/http.rs:2094`) = entries matching `(type, owner)` **ignoring** `limit`/`offset`; and `next_cursor` — previously **always** `null` — is now populated iff `!files.is_empty() && offset + files.len() < total` (`crates/server/src/http.rs:2269-2270`). Cursor token: `base64url-unpadded("1" ‖ "\|" ‖ <next_offset> ‖ "\|" ‖ <query_fp>)`, minted at `crates/server/src/http.rs:2120` and bound to the normalized `(type, sort, owner)` triple by `cursor_fp` (`:2105`). New `400` codes, on the NEW parameters only: `bad_sort`, `bad_owner`, `bad_cursor`, `cursor_query_mismatch`. |
| **What changed (client)** | `list_feed`'s return type moved from a bare `Vec<FeedEntryDto>` to the `FeedPageDto { entries, next_cursor, total }` envelope (`crates/client-app/src/dto.rs:120-134`), and `ListFeedRequest` gained `offset`/`cursor`/`owner_me` (`crates/client-app/src/dto.rs:85-101`). The UI renders a numbered pager (`crates/client-app/ui/src/core/pager.ts`; arithmetic in `crates/client-app/ui/src/core/paging.ts`). |
| **Why the SERVER change is backward compatible** | (a) **An old client's request is byte-identical and takes the same path.** `ListQuery` carries no `deny_unknown_fields` and every field is `Option` (`crates/server/src/http.rs:2045-2066`), so a pre-paging client sending only `type`/`limit` gets `offset = 0`, `sort = newest`, `owner_only = false` — exactly today's behaviour. (b) **The `limit` contract is byte-unchanged**: `q.limit.unwrap_or(50).min(200)` at `crates/server/src/http.rs:2219`. Shipped callers ask for `limit=200` (`tools/live-smoke/src/steps.rs:180`, `crates/client-e2e/tests/bundle_e2e.rs:701,879`) and must keep getting 200; lowering either number would be a tightening. (c) **The added response key cannot break a shipped reader**: `crates/client-app/src/commands/feed.rs` parses the body as an untyped `serde_json::Value` and reads only `files`, as do `tools/live-smoke/src/steps.rs:184-186` and `crates/client-e2e/tests/bundle_e2e.rs:701`. (d) **Populating `next_cursor` does not move the fixture.** `compat/fixtures/http/files_list.res.json` carries `"next_cursor": null`, and the comparator treats a frozen `null` as **key-existence-only** — `crates/compat/tests/http_wire.rs:810-811`: *"A frozen `null` only pins the KEY's existence (it was an absent Option)."* / `Value::Null => {}`. `assert_superset` walks only FROZEN keys, so the added `total` is invisible to it. (e) The new `400` codes fire only on parameters **no shipped client sends at all**, so they cannot reject an existing request. |
| **THE NEW-CLIENT / OLD-SERVER HAZARD (recorded, and already mitigated in the client)** | An **upgraded client against an un-upgraded server** (prod `41912da`) has all four new parameters **silently ignored** — `serde_urlencoded` drops what it does not know — and is served **page 1 forever**. A client that trusted its own `offset` would then render "page 5" showing page 1's contents, indistinguishably. The mitigation is keyed off the **ABSENCE of `total`**, which is unambiguous because the field is serialized unconditionally (`crates/server/src/http.rs:2094`, no `skip_serializing_if`): a client MUST read a missing `total` as *"this server does not paginate"*, render **no pager**, and never request `offset > 0`. Already implemented — `page_from_json` reports `total: None` for a body with no `total` key (`crates/client-app/src/commands/feed.rs:120-140`), `FeedPageDto.total` carries it across the seam (`crates/client-app/src/dto.rs:133`), and `shouldShowPager` returns `false` for `null` (`crates/client-app/ui/src/core/paging.ts:92`). The unknown-`type` early return is deliberately **not** confusable with an old server: it emits `total: 0`, not an absent `total` (`crates/server/src/http.rs:2216-2224`). |
| **The accepted paging skew (do not "fix" this quietly)** | Both sorts order on `files.updated_at`, which is **MUTABLE**: `finalize_version` bumps it (`crates/server/src/pg.rs:822`) and so does **every `add_wrap`**, i.e. every re-share (`crates/server/src/pg.rs:1205-1210`). Offset paging over a mutable key is therefore **neither skip-free nor duplicate-free**: a re-share landing mid-walk moves an item across a page boundary, and that item is seen twice or missed. **This is ACCEPTED.** The alternatives were rejected on this document's own rule: sorting on the immutable `created_at` would stop a re-shared file ever surfacing in the recipient's feed (a product regression for existing users), and adding a column touches frozen surface #9. The real behaviour is asserted, not assumed — `crates/server/tests/pg_store.rs:1341` and `crates/server/tests/file_records.rs:502` reproduce both the repeat and the skip. |
| **The CLIENT seam, and why it is not surface #10** | `list_feed` is a **Tauri-internal** command and `ui/dist` ships inside the same binary — it is not a wire contract between independently-versioned peers. Its only caller is `crates/client-app/ui/src/components/feed-screen.ts`. Even so it was widened, not broken: every new `ListFeedRequest` field is `#[serde(default)] Option<…>`, so an exe upgraded without a matching `ui/dist` rebuild still binds a `{filter, sort}`-only payload — pinned by `list_feed_request_binds_an_old_ui_dist_payload` (`crates/client-app/src/commands/feed.rs:857`). The client `limit` clamp `unwrap_or(50).min(200)` is byte-unchanged at `crates/client-app/src/commands/feed.rs:163`. **The client-side sort survives on the non-paginating path only** (`sort_entries_legacy`, `crates/client-app/src/commands/feed.rs:39`, gated at `:127`) — deliberately, because an old server also ignores the new `sort` parameter, so removing the client sort outright would have silently broken "Oldest first" for exactly the population this rule protects. |
| **How OLD data is still read** | Unchanged. No stored format is touched — this is request/response shape only. |
| **Fixture that proves it** | **No new fixture, and none was needed: no new BYTES format was introduced.** The existing `compat/fixtures/http/files_list.res.json` still passes unedited (`git diff -- compat/fixtures/` is empty) for the reason in row (d). Behaviour is pinned by `crates/server/tests/pg_store.rs:1185` (paging/sort/owner over real Postgres), `:2132` (cursor round-trip, cursor-vs-offset equivalence, every `400` code, `limit=200` still honoured, unknown type → `total: 0`), `crates/server/tests/file_records.rs:355,440` (MemoryStore equivalents, including the `file_id` tiebreak that makes the order total) and 11 client-side unit tests at `crates/client-app/src/commands/feed.rs:679-872`. |
| **Automatic on upgrade?** | Yes — code only, both halves, and the two halves are **independent**: an old client against a new server ignores the new keys; a new client against an old server disables paging on its own. No migration, no operator step. |
| **Performance note (no migration added, on purpose)** | `files_listing_idx ON files(file_type, updated_at DESC)` (`migrations/0001_baseline.sql:152`) cannot serve the new query — and could not serve the old one either. A covering index would touch frozen surface #9 and needs its own decision and its own entry here. The measurement is written out in full in [`docs/runbooks/prod-upgrade.md`](../runbooks/prod-upgrade.md) **§4.11 "F3a — the index evidence for the paginated `GET /v1/files` (open item, measured 2026-08-02)"** — a TRACKED file, deliberately **not** one of the gitignored `docs/` scratch session-handoff notes (`.gitignore:63-69`), which are kept out of the repo precisely because they go stale, and citing one from here would leave this row dangling on a fresh clone and on the VPS: `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` against a real Postgres at 5000 files / 5000 wraps with `docs/schema.sql` loaded verbatim — all four shapes plan as **Seq Scan on `files` + Hash Join on `file_key_wraps` + Sort**, at **1.0–2.1 ms per query**, plus one added full scan of the filtered set per request for the `COUNT` behind `total`. Synthetic dataset, **not** the real VPS. |

## 2026-08-02 — deployment surface (`scripts/install-server.sh`) — the installer now REFUSES an existing install by default

Not a byte format, so no fixture and no read path — but the same rule applies, and this is where it bit hardest: the previous behaviour destroyed **every client's ability to log in**, which is precisely the outcome the rule forbids. Logged next to the 2026-07-14 deployment-environment entry above for the same reason that one is here.

| | |
|---|---|
| **Commit** | *(working tree — uncommitted; F1 + F4 of the prod-upgrade loop)* |
| **Surface** | Deployment environment — `scripts/install-server.sh`, plus the shared unit-env parser now duplicated in five scripts |
| **The hole** | `install-server.sh` advertised itself as *"idempotent — safe to run again"*, and the obvious operator action — *re-run the installer to change a setting* — was the one that destroyed the deployment. With `--public` it **unconditionally deleted `<data_dir>/tls/{cert,key}.der` and `client-pins/`**, after which the server mints a **brand-new identity** (`crates/portable-server/src/pki.rs`) and every client that pinned the old certificate fails the handshake **permanently**, with no re-pin path and no admin escape hatch. Separately it **rotated the `maxsecu` role password on every run** and wrote the matching unit hundreds of lines later, with the build and two blocking interactive prompts in between — so a Ctrl-C left a live database whose working password existed **nowhere**. |
| **What changed** | **(1) An EXISTING-INSTALL PREFLIGHT** (`scripts/install-server.sh:703-939`) that runs **before** apt, before the multi-minute build and before anything touches Postgres. Detection is the OR of three independent signals (`:737-762`): the systemd unit exists; `<data_dir>/tls/cert.der` exists; the `maxsecu` database has a non-empty `users` table (probed by `psql_maxsecu_query`, `:428`, which `cd`s to `/tmp` — the `scripts/fingerprint.sh:131` idiom, adopted after a `sudo -u postgres` chdir failure silently voided every query in that script). Any signal ⇒ **refuse**, naming `upgrade-server.sh`, the systemd drop-in recipe, `backup-`/`restore-server.sh` and `--reset` (`:764-839`). **(2) `--force-overwrite-existing-install`** (`:229`) is the only way past the preflight, and it explicitly does **NOT** touch client trust. **(3) `--rotate-tls-identity`** (`:233`) is now the ONLY thing that deletes an existing `tls/{cert,key}.der` + `client-pins/` (`:1246-1277`); the unconditional `--public` deletion is **gone**. Rotating on a live box needs **both** flags, and the refusal prints the exact two-flag command line. **(4) The password rotation is idempotent** (`:1060-1167`): when the role exists **and** a `DATABASE_URL` recovered from the unit is **proven** to connect, it is reused verbatim and **no `ALTER ROLE` is issued at all** — the `ALTER ROLE` at `:1137` fires only when nothing usable could be recovered — plus a hard connectivity assertion at `:1158` that fails loudly **before** the unit is written at `:1477`. **(5) THE IDENTITY RECONCILIATION + REFUSAL** (`scripts/install-server.sh:575-686` and `:841-914`). `DATA_DIR` and `RUN_USER` used to be **guesses** (`${SUDO_USER:-$USER}` and `$RUN_HOME/maxsecu-server-data`), assigned once and never checked against the installed unit — while this is the only one of the five scripts that WRITES them back (`User=` at `:1495`, `Environment=MAXSECU_DATA_DIR=` at `:1506`). A box installed with `sudo bash …` as `ubuntu` and re-run from a root shell entered by `su -` (no `SUDO_USER`) guessed `/root/maxsecu-server-data`, so the preflight's cert probe and the step-9 TLS gate both looked in the wrong place, both reported "no certificate", and `--force-overwrite-existing-install` printed *"the TLS cert + client pins are KEPT"* while relocating the unit onto an empty directory — where the server **mints a new TLS identity**, locking out every pinned client and orphaning every blob. Now the unit is the truth: its `User=` and `MAXSECU_DATA_DIR` (falling back to `<WorkingDirectory>/maxsecu-server-data`, the binary's own default) are adopted **before** the preflight, and any disagreement with what the run computed **refuses outright, naming both values, with no override — `--force-overwrite-existing-install` does not unlock it and neither does `--rotate-tls-identity`**. Relocating a data dir is a `stop` + `mv` + drop-in operation, which the refusal prints. **(6) THE SAME CATASTROPHE WITHOUT A UNIT** (`scripts/install-server.sh:773`, refusal at `:964-1075`, conditional reassurance at `:1077-1114`). (5) can only reconcile against a unit, so on a box where the **unit is gone but the data dir and the database survived** — the state `scripts/backup-server.sh` routes operators into when it finds no unit — `IDENTITY_MISMATCH` stayed empty, `DATA_DIR` stayed the `${SUDO_USER:-$USER}` guess, the cert probe missed, the `users` signal alone let `--force-overwrite-existing-install` through, and the run printed *"The TLS cert + client pins … are NOT deleted … this run locks out no client"* **immediately before step 9 computed `HAVE_TLS_CERT=0` and minted a new identity**. Two changes: the cert probe is now kept as `HAVE_CERT_AT_DATA_DIR`, and that reassurance may be printed **only** when a certificate was **positively confirmed** at the resolved data dir — with no certificate the run says instead that a new identity **will** be minted and every pinned client locked out; and a **non-empty `users` table with no certificate at the resolved data dir is refused outright**, because a live server always has a certificate, so accounts existing while none is found means the data dir was not located. **No override flag**, for the same reason as (5): the honest remedy is to *state* the directory (`sudo env MAXSECU_DATA_DIR=… bash …`), which can only ever agree with the box and can never relocate it, while a genuinely destroyed data dir is a **restore** (`restore-server.sh`), not an install. |
| **Why it is backward compatible** | **It can only refuse, never destroy.** Every path it blocks previously ended in a permanent, unrecoverable client lockout, and the refusal costs the operator nothing but the time to read it (it precedes apt, the build and Postgres). Nothing an operator already has is altered: a genuine fresh install has none of the three signals; a **dead-box rebuild** (`scripts/restore-server.sh`) likewise has none and passes; both automated harnesses either `--reset` first (`scripts/test-full-install.ps1:62`) or provision a fresh distro (`scripts/lib/wsl-harness.ps1:71-124`), so neither needs the opt-out flag. The password change is a widening in the same sense: it issues strictly **fewer** writes than before and falls back to today's mint-and-`ALTER` behaviour whenever it cannot prove a credential. The identity refusal (5) is the same shape: on a box where the run and the unit AGREE — which is every run from the account that installed it — nothing about the run changes at all; where they disagree it refuses instead of relocating, and a dead box has no unit to disagree with, so `scripts/restore-server.sh` still sends the operator here safely. |
| **Also in this change (F4)** | The unit-environment parser `resolve_unit_env` (`Environment=` across the unit + drop-ins, then `EnvironmentFile=` as a fallback) is now **byte-identical in five scripts**: `scripts/install-server.sh:467`, `scripts/upgrade-server.sh:582`, `scripts/backup-server.sh:243`, `scripts/restore-server.sh:375`, `scripts/fingerprint.sh:79`. It replaces three weaker variants, each of which could **silently** read "unset": `backup-server.sh` had no `EnvironmentFile` fallback (a silent wrong-data-dir seal), `restore-server.sh` had the strictest regex in the repo on the **dead-box `DATABASE_URL` path**, and `fingerprint.sh` read the 0600 unit without root, so a non-root caller got a **default** data dir and a fingerprint that proved nothing. Pure widening — each copy can now find a value where the old one found none. It is deliberately **NOT** extracted to `scripts/lib/`: the server tree is delivered by SFTP drag-and-drop with no git, and a partial copy missing `scripts/lib/` would make `. missing-file` abort a **dead-box restore** under `set -euo pipefail`. See the deployment-surface section in [`CHECKLIST.md`](CHECKLIST.md) for the duplication contract and the known systemd-precedence deviation carried in all five copies. |
| **How OLD data is still read** | Not applicable — no format. Old boxes are unaffected until an operator runs the script, and then they are refused rather than damaged. |
| **Proven by** | 44 shell-level assertions across four throwaway harnesses, each driving the **verbatim** block extracted from the shipped script (flag parsing, preflight detection and refusal, the TLS gate, password reuse against a Postgres stub that models the role's password) — plus a **fifth** harness for (5), 7 cases over the verbatim `2b-0` block: a dead box (no unit) adopts nothing and raises no mismatch; the `su -` scenario adopts the unit's `User=` **and** `MAXSECU_DATA_DIR` and raises the mismatch on both; an agreeing unit raises none; a unit with no `MAXSECU_DATA_DIR` falls back to `<WorkingDirectory>/maxsecu-server-data`; a drop-in overriding either one wins (last assignment); indented and quoted directives still parse. The refusal block was driven separately and confirmed to print both values and `exit 1`. For (6), a **sixth** harness extracts the whole 2b-0 → 2b-pre → 2b-post → 2b-post2 → reassurance span as **one contiguous verbatim chunk** (so the real control flow, early exits included, is what runs) and drives 13 cases: a dead box with no unit / no dir / **no database at all** and one with `users = 0` both pass through untouched; a unit that agrees, and a unit-less box whose cert IS found, are allowed **and** print the "no client is locked out" line; a disagreeing unit and a `WorkingDirectory`-fallback unit refuse via 2b-post; **no unit + 3 users + no cert at the resolved dir refuses via 2b-post2**, and still refuses with `--rotate-tls-identity` added; the same state without the force flag refuses at 2b-pre while printing *"NOT the TLS certificate: none was found at …"* instead of the old "are KEPT"; a unit with no cert and no users is allowed but prints *"NO client trust is preserved by this run"*. Proven **non-vacuous** by re-running the identical harness against a scratchpad copy with (6) reverted: cases 5, 7, 8 and 10 fail there, case 5 by **proceeding (exit 0) while printing the false reassurance verbatim**. **No live box was provisioned** — the paths NOT exercised end to end are the real `sudo -u postgres` database probe and a real `--force-overwrite-existing-install` run. `crates/compat/tests/env_surface.rs` is unaffected: F1+F4 leave the `SERVER_ENV_SURFACE` table (`scripts/install-server.sh:357-373`, located by a LITERAL string match in `env_surface.rs`) byte-identical. Note it is **not** byte-identical to `HEAD` — one row moved, `MAXSECU_COLD_FS_DIR|default` → `MAXSECU_COLD_FS_DIR|unit-fs`, in the earlier `--cold-tier-fs` work in this same working tree, not in this change. The test is green either way. |
| **Automatic on upgrade?** | Not applicable — this is an operator tool, not a server code path. Nothing runs it automatically. |

## 2026-08-02 — CORRECTION to the 2026-08-01 entry (no surface moved) — "no trusted signing key anywhere" was imprecise

**Appended, not edited** — the entry above stays exactly as written, per this file's own rule. This corrects one factual claim inside it and records the decision that supersedes its forward-looking half.

| | |
|---|---|
| **Commit** | *(no code change; documentation only)* |
| **Surface** | None. Nothing moved. |
| **What was wrong** | The 2026-08-01 entry's *"What was deliberately NOT admitted (`add_wrap`)"* row says `granted_by = RECOVERY_ID` resolves to **"no trusted signing key anywhere"**, and the same wording spread into `DESIGN.md`, `docs/api.md`, the recovery spec, `docs/runbooks/recovery-session.md` and `docs/security-review-trusted-server-recovery.md`. **The recovery account DOES hold an Ed25519 `sig_pub`, server-side** — `crates/server/src/store.rs:47-51`, `RecoveryAccount { enc_pub, sig_pub, mlkem_pub }`. The accurate claim is **"no CLIENT-TRUSTED path to it"**: `GET /v1/recovery/pubkey` serves only `enc_pub_b64`/`mlkem_pub_b64` (`crates/server/src/http.rs:667-686`), the embedded recovery pin omits `sig_pub`, and every client open path passes no-op granter/admin resolvers — so the chain walk still ends in `GrantChainBroken`. |
| **Why the correction matters** | The conclusion is unchanged, but the imprecise version invites the **wrong fix**: someone reading "no signing key exists" would mint one server-side and believe the route was safe to open. It would not be — nothing would have given a *client* a reason to trust it. |
| **The decision, recorded** | **Sharing from a recovery session is a CLOSED DECISION (owner, 2026-08-02): it does not ship and is not pending.** The 2026-08-01 entry lists two prerequisites ("it may not ship until *both* of these exist"). Those two candidate designs — a published directory binding for `RECOVERY_ID` carrying a real Ed25519 signing key, or `sig_pub` added to the recovery pin (frozen surface #7) with the chain terminating at the `DESIGN.md` §12.7 admin key, **plus** a server-side refusal of a REPLACE when `granted_by == RECOVERY_ID` — **were declined by the operator.** Neither is scheduled. The load-bearing reason is unchanged and is the third one: `add_wrap` is idempotent **by REPLACE** in both stores (`crates/server/src/store.rs:1228`; `crates/server/src/pg.rs:1184-1203`), so a recovery re-share to somebody who already had access destroys it. Regranting access is the air-gapped `DESIGN.md` §12.7 ceremony's job (`docs/runbooks/recovery-session.md`). |
| **Direction** | Still not a tightening: nothing ever shipped admitting `add_wrap`, so no deployed caller's outcome changes. Shipping it later would be the widening, and it would still need its own entry here. |

## 2026-08-03 — DB schema (#9) — migration `0003` adds a HASH index on `auth_nonces (username) WHERE used_at IS NULL`

| | |
|---|---|
| **Commit** | *(working tree — uncommitted; the `sessions`-growth investigation of the prod-upgrade loop)* |
| **Surface** | #9, DB schema — `migrations/0003_auth_nonce_lookup.sql`, mirrored into `docs/schema.sql`, re-pinned in `compat/schema.lock` (`schema` digest, new `0003` line, `schema_head 2 → 3`) |
| **What changed** | One statement: `CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS auth_nonces_open_idx ON auth_nonces USING hash (username) WHERE used_at IS NULL;` — it matches `PgStore::outstanding_nonces` (`crates/server/src/pg.rs`), whose predicate carries `used_at IS NULL` verbatim. No column, constraint, trigger, row or query changes. Before this, `auth_nonces` had exactly one index (the primary key on `nonce`), so **every login seq-scanned the whole table**. |
| **Why it is backward compatible** | An index is invisible to SQL semantics: an OLD binary against a migrated database and a NEW binary against an un-migrated one both return identical rows, because **the query is not changed at all**. Nothing is rejected that was accepted before. `upgrade-server.sh` stops the server before applying migrations and starts it after, so the `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE` lock taken by the plain `CREATE INDEX` is free — and it must be the plain form, because `migrations/apply.sh` wraps every migration in `BEGIN;`/`COMMIT;` and hard-refuses a file containing its own transaction control, while `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` cannot run inside a transaction. |
| **WHY `USING hash`, AND NOT THE OBVIOUS BTREE — this is the load-bearing row** | The first draft of this migration was a btree, it passed the whole gate green, and it **would have permanently blocked the upgrade on a real box.** `auth_nonces.username` is unbounded `TEXT` on rows already on disk and `nonce_key_col` hex-encodes it, doubling the stored length; a btree entry is capped at 2704 bytes. An abandoned challenge keeps `used_at IS NULL` **forever**, so it sits *inside* the partial index. Reproduced against PG 14.13 by applying the real file through the real `apply.sh` on a database holding one such row: `ERROR: index row requires 128016 bytes, maximum size is 8191`, `apply-exit=1`. `apply.sh` then fails, `upgrade-server.sh` restores the previous binary and exits — and **no later migration can repair it, because the failure is at `0003` itself**, so a `0004` would never run. The only exit would be a human hand-deleting a row from Postgres, on a box that has no admin escape hatch by design. A hash index hashes the value and therefore has **no entry-size ceiling at all**, and it serves exactly the equality this lookup does, with **no query change**. A bounded-projection btree (`left()` / `md5()`) was rejected: it would force the login hot-path SQL to carry a second conjunct that must stay in sync with the index definition forever, and would re-introduce an index-side ceiling to reconcile against. A delete-guard inside the migration was rejected outright — see the next row. |
| **THE RESTORE PATH IS WHY A MIGRATION-TIME CLEANUP CANNOT WORK** | `backup::merge::merge_auth_nonces` inserts a bundle's `username` values **verbatim, at restore time, into an already-`0003` database**, inside the single transaction the whole restore runs in. A row arriving from a six-month-old bundle is unreachable by any cleanup done at migration time, so a delete-guard would have closed the upgrade path and left **disaster recovery** — the one path that must never be able to fail — still broken. Separately, "safe to delete" is not decidable: a bundle-carried row's `expires_at` is whatever that box wrote, and deleting an unexpired row is exactly the tightening [`CHECKLIST.md`](CHECKLIST.md) forbids. |
| **How OLD data is still read** | Unchanged — no stored format is touched. Both readers already discard everything the index concerns: `crates/server/src/auth.rs` treats an expired or revoked session as absent, and `crates/server/src/pg.rs` filters `used_at IS NULL AND expires_at > $2`. |
| **Fixture that proves it** | No new fixture: no new BYTES format was introduced, and `git diff compat/fixtures/` is empty. Proven instead by `crates/compat/tests/schema_equivalence.rs` (5/5 against a live Postgres — `compat_fresh_install_equals_upgraded_install` proves `docs/schema.sql` and baseline+migrations produce an **identical catalog**), and by `merge_restores_a_bundle_carrying_an_unindexable_nonce_username` in `crates/server/tests/backup_merge.rs`, which is **load-bearing**: reverting the index to btree makes it fail with the real restore aborting (`index row requires 128016 bytes`), not with a fixture-setup error. |
| **Exact equality is preserved, and it was proven rather than cited** | A hash index can return false positives that the recheck must drop. Real 32-bit `hashtext` collisions were brute-forced (e.g. `user277525` / `user286027`) and driven through both plan shapes: `Bitmap Heap Scan` and plain `Index Scan` each report `Rows Removed by Index Recheck: 1` and return **only the correct row**. An exhaustive differential over all 5 021 distinct usernames in an 80 021-row database found **0 mismatches** between index-scan and seq-scan results. The index does not normalize: NFC and NFD spellings of the same name stay two distinct rows. Crash safety was verified rather than assumed — `CHECKPOINT`, 20 000 inserts, `pg_ctl stop -m immediate`, restart: WAL redo replayed and all 20 000 rows were still reachable through the index. |
| **Automatic on upgrade?** | Yes — migration `0003`, applied by `scripts/upgrade-server.sh` while the server is stopped. Measured effect on the login lookup at 50 000 rows: `Seq Scan`, 618 buffers, 4.294 ms becomes `Index Scan`, 2 buffers, 0.051 ms. The partial predicate keeps it tiny — 16 kB against a 4 944 kB heap, because only unconsumed challenges are indexed. |

## 2026-08-03 — `/v1` HTTP JSON (#10) — TIGHTENING: an absurdly long `username` is refused on `/v1/session/challenge` and `/v1/session/proof`

| | |
|---|---|
| **Commit** | *(working tree — uncommitted)* |
| **Surface** | #10, `/v1` HTTP JSON — `POST /v1/session/challenge` and `POST /v1/session/proof` |
| **What changed** | Both routes now reject a `username` longer than `MAX_SESSION_USERNAME_BYTES = 4 * maxsecu_encoding::MAX_TEXT` (4096 raw bytes) **before anything is written**, using the route's existing bad-request shape. |
| **The hole it closes** | Neither route bounded the claimed username, and **neither requires authentication**. A single request could write a multi-megabyte `auth_nonces` row that nothing ever deleted; issuance is capped per *claimed username* with no per-IP cap, so a prober cycling names could write roughly 15.8 M immortal rows per year per name. The `proof` route additionally keys an in-memory rate-limiter map that is **never evicted**, so one request permanently allocated its username. |
| **Why this tightening cannot lock anybody out — the argument, not the assertion** | The bound is provably above every username that **can exist**. Account creation (`POST /v1/users`) validates through `Text::new`, which accepts a name iff its **NFC form** is at most `MAX_TEXT` (1024 bytes), but stores the **raw** bytes. The maximum ratio of raw length to NFC length over all of UTF-8 is exactly **3** (the singleton U+212A KELVIN SIGN maps to `K`, 3 bytes to 1; fully-decomposed Hangul L+V+T is 9 to 3; the longest Greek-Extended decomposition is only 8 to 3). So no storable name can exceed `3 * MAX_TEXT` raw bytes, and the limit is `4 * MAX_TEXT` — a whole `MAX_TEXT` of margin above the true ceiling. This is pinned by a test that constructs the actual worst case (`"\u{212A}".repeat(MAX_TEXT)`, asserted to be exactly `3 * MAX_TEXT` bytes and to pass `Text::new`) and shows it is still accepted. **The reconciliation with the index is that there is no second limit to reconcile against**: `0003` is a hash index with no entry-size ceiling, so there is no band of names the HTTP bound accepts and the index rejects — which is exactly the class of defect this pairing could otherwise have created. |
| **Direction** | A genuine tightening of a frozen surface, recorded as such. It changes the outcome only for a request no real account could ever make, and it converts an unauthenticated permanent write into a `400`. |
| **How OLD data is still read** | Unaffected — no stored format, and rows already on disk are never re-validated. Over-long rows that already exist keep being read, and are removed only by expiry through the prune below. |
| **Automatic on upgrade?** | Yes — code only, no migration, no operator step. |

---

## 2026-08-03 — server behaviour (no frozen surface moved) — a bounded, EXPIRY-ONLY prune for `sessions` and `auth_nonces`

| | |
|---|---|
| **Commit** | *(working tree — uncommitted)* |
| **Surface** | **None of the twelve.** A `DELETE` in Rust code is not a stored format and not a schema object. Recorded here because these two tables had **never** had a row deleted by anything, and because the *shape* of the predicate is a compatibility question even though the change itself is not. |
| **What changed** | A background task on a one-hour tick (`spawn_auth_prune`, wired in `crates/portable-server/src/run.rs`) deletes, in bounded batches of `AUTH_PRUNE_BATCH = 5 000`, rows whose `expires_at` is older than `AUTH_PRUNE_GRACE_MS = 7 days`. No cron and no systemd timer — the box has zero timer surface today and is delivered by SFTP drag-and-drop with no git, so adding ops surface was rejected. |
| **The three properties that make it safe, and why each is load-bearing** | **(1) EXPIRY-ONLY.** The predicate must never key on `revoked_at` or on `used_at`. The restore MERGE re-inserts a bundle's copy with a bare `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`, so deleting a *revoked* row removes the thing the merge relies on to lose — and the bundle's pre-logout copy would come back **un-revoked**, resurrecting a signed-out session. Expiry-only makes that impossible, because anything prunable is already dead to every reader. **(2) A 7-DAY GRACE**, which is 168 times the one-hour session TTL and 10 080 times the 60-second nonce TTL; runtime assertions require the grace to dwarf both. **(3) NEVER prune an unexpired row** — that is the one shape that would be a tightening, because it would sign out a user who is still working. |
| **Why it is backward compatible** | Both readers already treat every prunable row as non-existent — `crates/server/src/auth.rs` returns `Unauthorized` for an expired session, and `crates/server/src/pg.rs` filters `expires_at > $2`. An old binary meeting a pruned table therefore observes **bit-identical** behaviour. A prune failure is logged and retried on the next tick and can never fail a login. |
| **Correcting the record on WHY this was needed** | The prod-upgrade handoff states that the `sessions` table "grew 334 to 358 rows while merely sitting there". **That is false, and the code cannot produce it**: a row is inserted only inside a completed challenge/proof over a live TLS channel, and there is no timer, cron, trigger or background task anywhere that could add one. Measured on the live gate1 box before it was destroyed: over **eleven idle hours the table grew by zero rows**; the 24 rows were a burst of real activity. Growth is per **TLS channel mint** (about 5 to 6 per app open), not per unit of time — and not per authed command either, since a minted channel is reused for 20 minutes. Disk was never the problem: a realistic year is about 13 MB and a heavy one about 83 MB. **The actual defect was the missing index above**; the prune exists to keep that index, and the table, permanently small. |
| **Automatic on upgrade?** | Yes — code only, starts with the server. |

## 2026-08-03 — deployment surface (`scripts/install-server.sh`) — seven holes in the existing-install guard, closed

| | |
|---|---|
| **Commit** | *(working tree — uncommitted; step 1 of the prod-upgrade loop)* |
| **Surface** | Deployment environment — `scripts/install-server.sh`. Same reasoning as the 2026-08-02 entry above: not a byte format, but the failure it prevents is a permanent, unrecoverable client lockout. |
| **The holes** | The 2026-08-02 preflight was real but **incomplete**. Seven ways past it, all found by *executing* the shipped script rather than reading it — reading it had already been done twice, by agents that concluded it was safe. **(1) The guard could go completely SILENT.** Detection is the OR of three signals; signal 3 probed the `users` table **hundreds of lines before the script starts PostgreSQL**, the helper swallowed every error, and the classifier read empty as zero. With no unit, PostgreSQL stopped, and the data dir not at the guessed path, all three signals read absent, the run proceeded with **no flag typed at all**, and minted a new TLS identity. That is the original catastrophe, post-fix, with zero opt-in. **(2) `--reset` was a bigger, entirely unguarded version of the same thing** — it ran hundreds of lines before the preflight, deleted the unit (the only copy of the database password) **first**, skipped the `DROP` when PostgreSQL was down, `rm -rf`'d a **guessed** data dir, and printed "back to zero" while the real `tls/cert.der` and `tls/key.der` survived — leaving precisely the state hole 1 mis-reads as fresh. **(3)** `README.md` answered the 409 "recovery account already registered" — which is what a **healthy, fully-set-up server** returns — by routing the operator to the full reset, with no inline caveat. **(4)** The refusal's last copy-pasteable line was the destructive two-flag command. **(5)** `ALTER ROLE` rotated a **live** role with no INT/TERM trap, and the abort that followed claimed "no data was touched", which was false on that path. **(6)** Five `psql` calls used a bare `-h localhost` with **no port** — the string `5432` appeared nowhere in the 2004-line file — while the `DATABASE_URL` it had just built was ignored. **(7)** `cert.der` present with `key.der` absent was a **false reassurance on both screens**: the server requires both, so it silently minted a new identity while the script promised "every installed client stays connected". |
| **What changed** | The users signal is now **tri-state** — `absent` / `known` / `indeterminate` — and "I could not find out" is no longer read as "there is nothing there": the run starts PostgreSQL purely to look (`systemctl start`, never `enable --now`, so the boot configuration is untouched), waits on **actual connectability** against a real wall-clock deadline, and **refuses** if it still cannot ask. The narrow `--assume-no-database` is the only way past that, and its help text says in plain words that it forfeits the accounts check. The TLS probes now test **cert AND key**, and a half-present identity is reported as **BROKEN** — refusing rather than promising continuity it cannot deliver — while still contributing to `EXISTING_SIGNALS`, so **detection remains an OR** and a cert-only box is never silently treated as fresh. `--reset` now resolves the **real** data dir from the unit *before* deleting the unit, destroys in a safe order, keeps the unit when the `DROP` cannot be **proven** (re-probed, not trusted to an exit status), asks the operator to type `DESTROY` when there is a terminal, and reports honestly — it prints "back to zero" only when that is true, and otherwise enumerates exactly what survived, including any other TLS identity found elsewhere on the box. When the role exists but no working password can be recovered, the installer now **refuses and prints the two repair recipes** instead of rotating a live role — which removes the dangerous window rather than shrinking it, and makes it agree with `upgrade-server.sh`, which already told operators not to re-run the installer in that state. Database host and port are taken from the installed unit (defaulting to `127.0.0.1:5432`) and threaded through **every** `psql` call, with the cluster's real port discovered when it is not the default. The final banner reports **state, not flags** — it reads the certificate's SANs rather than asserting an address it never looked at. |
| **Why it is backward compatible** | **It can only refuse, never destroy.** Every path it newly blocks previously ended in a permanent client lockout, and every refusal precedes apt, the build, and any write. A genuine fresh install is unaffected — verified by *running* it: `--public <IP> --port <n>` with no other flags exits 0 on a brand-new box, mints an identity, applies all three migrations, and leaves the service active with `NRestarts=0`. `--reset` unattended still exits 0 with **no new flag**, deliberately, so `scripts/lib/wsl-harness.ps1` and the existing runbook invocations keep working; `--reset` on a never-installed box still exits 0. |
| **Proven by** | **Executed, not read** — the same standard that found the holes. On a throwaway WSL box restored from a pristine snapshot before each run, each hole was driven with the **fixed** script and then, in the identical state, with the **pre-fix** script as a negative control, so the test is shown to be able to fail. Hole 1: the fixed run refuses (exit 1) and mints nothing while the real identity survives; the pre-fix run exits 0 and mints `f5f54474…` over the real `61eb6028…`, locking out every client. Hole 7: the fixed run reports "key.der is MISSING — a BROKEN identity"; the pre-fix run prints "are KEPT — no client is locked out" and never mentions the key at all. Hole 5: the fixed run refuses with the repair recipe and the original password still authenticates; the pre-fix run exits 0 and it **no longer does**. Hole 2: the fixed `--reset` destroys the unit-declared `/srv/…` directory rather than the guessed one, and prints "NOT back to zero" with a full inventory of what survived. Alongside these, harnesses that execute the shipped spans byte-for-byte against stubs, including a 24 164-case fuzz differential of the new IP-literal validator against openssl's own parser (**zero** accepted-but-unparseable addresses). |
| **How OLD data is still read** | Not applicable — no format. Old boxes are unaffected until an operator runs the script, and then they are refused rather than damaged. |
| **Automatic on upgrade?** | Not applicable — an operator tool; nothing runs it automatically. |

## 2026-08-03 — CORRECTION to the 2026-08-02 `install-server.sh` entry (no surface moved)

**Appended, not edited** — the entry above stays exactly as written, per this file's own rule. It records what was true when it was written. Four of its statements have since been made false **by the change above**, and its line numbers have drifted. Both are recorded here so a future reader is not misled by either.

| | |
|---|---|
| **Commit** | *(no code change; documentation only)* |
| **Surface** | None. Nothing moved. |
| **Statements in the 2026-08-02 entry that the 2026-08-03 change has since made FALSE** | (a) "the refusal prints the exact two-flag command line" — it no longer does, deliberately: that was hole 4. The refusal now says the command is **not** pasted, tells the operator to read the README section first, and the last copy-pasteable line it prints is the **safe** one (`upgrade-server.sh`). (b) "falls back to today's mint-and-`ALTER` behaviour whenever it cannot prove a credential", and the reference to "the `ALTER ROLE`" — there is **no executable `ALTER ROLE` left in the file**; that path is now a refusal with a printed repair recipe. (c) "the cert probe is now kept as `HAVE_CERT_AT_DATA_DIR`", and the reassurance keyed on it — the reassurance is now keyed on the **pair** (`HAVE_IDENTITY_AT_DATA_DIR`), because a certificate without its key is a broken identity, not a kept one. (d) The three-signal description is still accurate in shape, but signal 2 now reads `cert.der` **OR** `key.der`, and signal 3 is tri-state rather than a count. |
| **Line numbers** | **Every `scripts/install-server.sh` line number in the 2026-08-02 entry is stale**, and so are the ones in `CHECKLIST.md` and `docs/runbooks/prod-upgrade.md` written before 2026-08-03. The file went from 2004 to 3763 lines in this change alone, and had already drifted by +17 before that, when the `--cold-tier-fs` arms were inserted. **Do not trust a line number in any entry above this one.** They are left byte-untouched on purpose: this file is append-only, and an entry is a record of what was written, not a live index. |
| **The rule going forward** | Cite a **stable anchor string** — a distinctive comment banner (`# 2b-pre0.`), a `case` arm (`--rotate-tls-identity)`), a function name — not a line number. Line numbers in this repo have gone stale silently every single time anyone edited these scripts, and a stale citation reads exactly like a correct one. |
